scope: Twenty-fourth expansion batch: 12 controlled past-expectation exercises. Three earlier forward expectations contrast with three current inferences about completed past events, using arrive/begin/go-out. Six recollection-context items contrast three expected occurrences with three expected nonoccurrences, using come/ring/rain. Explicit recollection permits fulfilled outcomes without treating every isolated V-ru hazu-datta as a neutral past forecast.

sources.publisher: Park Cheonhong (朴天弘), University of Tokyo Graduate School of Arts and Sciences, Language and Information Sciences 10 (2012), pp. 55-71
sources.section: Actual repository record identifies the title 条件文と非条件文における「ハズ」の反事実的な意味の一考察 : 「スル+はずだった」を中心に, author, journal and pages. Actual PDF https://repository.dl.itc.u-tokyo.ac.jp/record/16547/files/lis01004.pdf inspected: abstract p.55; tense comparison (2'a-d) p.56; section 3.2, especially p.63 example23 and (19''-22'') on memory-confirmation contexts/tashika suppressing a required counterfactual reading, and pp.64-66 explaining the common disappointed-expectation reading and its relation to prior information. Recollection is a contextual interpretation, not a claim that inserting tashika always guarantees truth or fulfillment. The source supports the pattern distinction, not independent attestation of our invented sentences.

sources.publisher: Tae Kim's Guide to Learning Japanese
sources.section: Actual Using hazu to describe an expectation section: attachment chart, example1 with yonda-hazu and example2 with oishii-hazu-datta and a disappointing outcome. The text's claim that a negative expectation must use hazu-ga/wa-nai is overbroad and is NOT adopted; a negative embedded predicate can precede hazu. Its broad restrictions on beki advice and suggested certainty scales elsewhere are outside this batch.

Actual heading Should / hazu-da and predicate chart; example2 tsuku-hazu-datta, example4 konde-inai-hazu alongside positive alternatives, example8 yatta-hazu and example9 todoite-iru-hazu. These support past expectation, embedded negation, completed-event inference and the existence of result-state alternatives. Some unrelated sample translations/physical claims are not adopted.

Actual hazu-datta examples with counterfactual conditions and disappointed trip/exam/weather expectations. These illustrate the common unfulfilled use, not proof that all past hazu clauses require failure; Park's explicit recollection discussion provides the qualification.
Exact 届く/todoku, godan-ku intransitive, delivered/arrive sense; not the figurative fulfilled-desire sense. Corresponding past todoita is the completion form.
Exact 始まる/hajimaru, godan-ru intransitive begin/start sense; not transitive hajimeru or the recurrent-behavior sense.
Exact 消える/kieru, ichidan intransitive, sense2 for light/fire going out; not a person's disappearance. The corresponding event past is kieta.
Exact 来る/kuru, special kuru-verb intransitive come/arrive sense, not the auxiliary after te-form. The negative is konai, not kunai.
Exact 鳴る/naru, godan-ru intransitive sound/ring. Distinguish transitive narasu in the setting description and the unrelated become verb.
Exact 降る/furu, godan-ru intransitive, rain/snow falling sense; not oriru or the metaphorical arrival of fortune.

authoringNotes: All exercises are original. Consequential tense/recollection distinctions were checked against the actual university paper, not a search summary. Its theoretical account is one analysis, not a universal classification of every hazu use; the batch adopts only the scoped construction and context distinctions.

The first six tasks visibly name dictionary-form verb + kana hazu-datta versus ta-form verb + kana hazu-da. Their question-side time references and instructions distinguish an earlier forward expectation from a present inference about a completed event. The latter is not a normative should-have judgment or direct verification. Result-state te-iru, other tense combinations, polite endings and whole-sentence paraphrases remain outside these named patterns, not globally wrong.

The three earlier-forward items include two disappointed forecasts and one explicit memory-confirmation context later shown to be fulfilled. The fulfilled light example quotes the attendant's thought before the expected evening action, avoiding a free-floating past forecast followed by an unexplained reversal of its ordinary frustrated-expectation implication.

All six polarity items supply hazu-datta and reconstruct the predicate inside an explicitly located earlier recollection with omoidasu and tashika. They accept dictionary or nai forms of the supplied verb in kana/kanji. Three positive forecasts include two fulfillments and one failure; three negative forecasts include two fulfillments and one surprise. The visitor arrives in both visitor items and the chime stays silent in both chime items, preventing outcome-based polarity guessing.

A recollection marker does not establish truth. The negative-attendance recollection is later contradicted, and the positive chime recollection is frustrated. Conversely, hazu-datta does not automatically require failure in these explicit recollection contexts. Avoid flattening either qualification into an unconditional rule.

A negative embedded predicate expresses expected nonoccurrence, not prohibition, inability or an arbitrary confidence threshold. These exercises do not claim that V-nai-hazu and V-ru-hazu-ga-nai are globally interchangeable. The weather contexts distinguish a forecast from a wish or guarantee.

The full article inventory and existing intent/foundation hazu exercises were screened. New IDs add focused tense, polarity and outcome coverage without rewriting the earlier hazu/you shared inferences or their answer classes. Broader mixed selection, nonverbal past expectations and all recollection/conditional uses are not claimed as complete coverage.

Retrieval limits: Bunpro's guessed hazu-datta URL returned404, and its actual hazu-da page did not establish the needed past exception. Weblio simplified extraction exposed headings only. Early web-search summaries paired titles with different URLs and attributed unsupported text to dictionaries or scholarly papers; those claims were discarded. The actual DOI/repository PDF above, not the unverified Kyoto links, supplied the consequential evidence. A TUFS directory URL returned403. The actual UTokyo BiblioPlaza author summary was also inspected but does not replace the paper's precise examples.

All305 earlier exercise records and IDs remain unchanged. The learner article gains one scoped subsection and one new reference bullet; README, contract and focused regressions describe the same bounded tasks. No Android schema, UI, grading, counter or SRS behavior changes; every exercise has one identity and one representative correct button.
